item.statement_excerpt:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $S=\mathbb R_s\times[0,1]_t$ and $m\ge1$. Let $\mathcal X_{\mathbb R}^1$ be the real $H^1$ completion of smooth maps compactly supported in $s$ with values in $\mathbb R^m$ on both horizontal edges. Choose a smooth $\rho\ge0$ equal to $|s|$ for $|s|\ge1$, with $|\rho'|\le1$ and bounded derivatives of every positive order, and let $w=e^{\delta\rho}$ for $0<\delta<\pi$. Put $H^q_\delta=w^{-1}H^q$ and $\mathcal X^1_{\mathbb R,\delta}=w^{-1}\mathcal X^1_{\mathbb R}$. Fix a smooth real cutoff $\chi_+$ equal to zero for $s\le-1$ and one for $s\ge1$, and put $\chi_-=1-\chi_+$.

For every integer $q\ge0$ define the real Hilbert domain of maps with free real end constants by
$$\mathcal E_q=\{u=r+\chi_-c_-+\chi_+c_+:\ r\in H^{q+1}_\delta\cap\mathcal X^1_{\mathbb R,\delta},\ c_-,c_+\in\mathbb R^m\},$$
with norm $\|wr\|_{H^{q+1}}+|c_-|+|c_+|$ or its equivalent squared-sum Hilbert norm. This representation is unique. The actual operator
$$D_0=\partial_s+i\partial_t:\mathcal E_q\longrightarrow H^q_\delta$$
is bounded and onto, has kernel exactly the global real constant maps, and has real Fredholm index $m$. It has a specified bounded right inverse $Q_q$ whose solutions have $c_-=0$; these right inverses agree on their common domains. For $u\in\mathcal E_0$ and $f=D_0u$, the exact matching identity is
$$c_+-c_-=\int_{\mathbb R}f_0(s)\,ds,\qquad f_0(s)=\operatorname{Re}\int_0^1 f(s,t)\,dt.$$
In particular a solution with both end constants zero exists exactly when this real integral is zero, and is then unique. At higher orders only the zeroth real boundary trace is imposed; no normal-derivative or forcing trace is added. This is the actual linear same-boundary neck model. It asserts no geometric boundary-degeneration classification or nonlinear gluing theorem.

proof_step_donor_fragments.exact_current_text: The functions $e_n(t)=e^{-i\pi nt}$, $n\in\mathbb Z$, are a complete real orthonormal basis of $L^2([0,1];\mathbb C)$. Real orthogonality is $\operatorname{Re}\int_0^1e_n\overline{e_k}=\delta_{nk}$. For completeness extend $v$ to $[-1,1]$ by $v(-t)=\overline{v(t)}$ and then with period two. Its complex Fourier coefficients are real, by substituting $t\mapsto-t$ and conjugating, and [F1] gives its complete expansion. Restricting gives exactly the asserted real expansion. The zero coefficient is $v_0=\operatorname{Re}\int_0^1v$. For smooth maps in the defining real-boundary domain, integration by parts in $t$ gives the coefficient of $i\partial_t v$ equal to $\pi n v_n$: the boundary term has zero real part since both endpoint values and $e_n$ there are real. Thus Parseval gives $$\|v_t\|_2^2=\sum_n\pi^2n^2\|v_n\|_{L^2_s}^2,\qquad (D_0v)_n=v_n'+\pi n v_n.$$ The same assertions pass to its $H^1$ completion. Conversely scalar $H^1(\mathbb R)$ coefficients with the summed $H^1$ and displayed derivative bounds reconstruct an element of that completion: first truncate in $n$, then approximate the finitely many coefficients in $H^1$ by longitudinal cutoff and convolution. Each resulting finite smooth sum has the required real edge values. This also proves the assertions on $\mathbb C^m$ componentwise, without assuming extra normal traces. [F1, construct, algebra]

On the subspace with zero coefficient zero, $D_0$ has a bounded unweighted inverse $T:L^2_\perp\to H^1_\perp\cap\mathcal X^1_{\mathbb R}$ and $\|Tf\|_2\le\pi^{-1}\|f\|_2$. Indeed for $\lambda=\pi n>0$ solve $a'+\lambda a=f_n$ by $a(s)=\int_{-\infty}^s e^{-\lambda(s-r)}f_n(r)\,dr$; for $\lambda<0$ use $a(s)=-\int_s^\infty e^{-\lambda(s-r)}f_n(r)\,dr$. These kernels have integral norm $1/|\lambda|$, so Cauchy–Schwarz against the kernel followed by integration gives $\|a\|_2\le|\lambda|^{-1}\|f_n\|_2$. Also $a'=f_n-\lambda a$, hence $\|a'\|_2\le2\|f_n\|_2$. Summing gives the $H^1$ bound and membership by step 1.1. A homogeneous mode is $ce^{-\lambda s}$, never in whole-line $L^2$ unless $c=0$; the scalar integrating-factor assertion follows for weak $H^1$ solutions from their one-dimensional weak primitive identity. Thus the inverse is two-sided. All sums converge by Parseval and completeness. [F1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

For the zero forcing coefficient $f_0\in L^2_\delta(\mathbb R;\mathbb R^m)$ the real integral $F=\int_\mathbb R f_0$ exists and satisfies $|F|\le\|w^{-1}\|_{L^2_s}\|wf_0\|_2$. Put $$a_0(s)=\int_{-\infty}^s f_0(r)\,dr,\qquad r_0=a_0-\chi_+F.$$ On $s\le-1$, $w(s)a_0(s)=\int_{-\infty}^s e^{-\delta(s-r)}w(r)f_0(r)\,dr$. On $s\ge1$, $w(s)(a_0(s)-F)=-\int_s^\infty e^{-\delta(r-s)}w(r)f_0(r)\,dr$. Each one-sided kernel has integral norm $1/\delta$, so the same elementary convolution estimate bounds the two weighted $L^2$ tails by $\delta^{-1}\|wf_0\|_2$. On $[-1,1]$ the integral Cauchy–Schwarz bound and the finite coefficient norms give the same estimate with a fixed larger constant. Finally $r_0'=f_0-\chi_+'F$ and $(wr_0)'=w(f_0-\chi_+'F)+\delta\rho'wr_0$. Thus $wr_0\in H^1$ with norm at most $C\|wf_0\|_2$. Since it is real and independent of $t$, it belongs to the required boundary completion by real longitudinal approximation. The map $a_0=r_0+\chi_+F$ consequently lies in $\mathcal E_0$, solves its actual zero-mode equation, and has end constants $0,F$. [step 1.1, construct, algebra]

The same nonzero-mode equation is invertible with weight $w$. If $v=wu$, conjugation gives $wD_0w^{-1}v=D_0v-\delta\rho'v$. Multiplication by $\rho'$ preserves the zero-coefficient complement and has $L^2$ norm at most one. Therefore the specified equation $$v=T(wf+\delta\rho'v)$$ is a contraction in $L^2_\perp$ of ratio at most $\delta/\pi<1$. Its geometric iteration gives the unique $L^2$ solution and the bound $\|v\|_2\le(\pi-\delta)^{-1}\|wf\|_2$. The same equation and the $L^2\to H^1$ bound of step 2.1 put it in $H^1\cap\mathcal X^1_{\mathbb R}$ with a bounded norm. Conversely any weighted solution obeys this equation, so uniqueness holds. Denote this actual weighted nonzero-mode inverse by $T_\delta$. Its construction used the gap $\pi$ only on the complement; it made no inverse assertion on the missing zero mode. [step 2.1, construct, algebra]

The representation in $\mathcal E_0$ is unique. If two representations agree, their remainder difference is weighted $L^2$, whereas on each end it equals the corresponding difference of their constant vectors. A nonzero constant on either infinite end is not weighted $L^2$, so both constant differences vanish, then the remainders coincide. Define $$Q_0f=T_\delta(f-f_0)+a_0,$$ using steps 3.1 and3.1. Its remainder and two constants have the asserted bounded norm, it has $c_-=0$, and direct modal differentiation gives $D_0Q_0f=f$. Boundedness of $D_0:\mathcal E_0\to L^2_\delta$ follows by differentiating its remainder and its fixed constant cutoffs; the weighted derivative uses only bounded $\rho'$. For any solution the zero coefficient has derivative $f_0$, and its weighted remainder tends to zero at each end in the weak one-dimensional $H^1$ sense. To check the latter without importing a trace theorem, a scalar $H^1$ function on each unit interval has supremum bounded by its $H^1$ norm there, by the fundamental theorem for its weak primitive and Cauchy–Schwarz; those interval norms tend to zero along either tail by integrability. The smooth weight then gives the claimed zero limit for the original remainder. Integrating its zero-mode derivative yields exactly $c_+-c_-=F$. In the homogeneous case this coefficient is constant and the nonzero component vanishes by step 3.1; the kernel is exactly the global real constants. Thus the solution with prescribed left constant zero is unique. [step 1.1, step 3.1, step 2.2, construct, algebra]

We prove the full higher regularity, including the domain issue, rather than imposing extra traces. Scalar differentiation and the Leibniz rule make $\|wv\|_{H^k}$ equivalent to $\sum_{|\alpha|\le k}\|w\partial^\alpha v\|_2$ for each fixed $k$: all logarithmic derivatives of $w$ and $w^{-1}$ are bounded. Let $D_0u=f\in H^1_\delta$ with $u=Q_0f$. Longitudinal difference quotients have zero end constants and preserve the real $H^1$ boundary completion. They solve $D_0\delta_hu=\delta_hf$, so uniqueness at left constant zero gives $\delta_hu=Q_0\delta_hf$. The weighted fundamental theorem gives $\|w\delta_hf\|_2\le e^{\delta|h|}\|wf_s\|_2$. Also $\int(\delta_h f)_0=0$, by translation invariance of the absolutely convergent zero-mode integral; therefore the output has both constants zero and its entire weighted $H^1$ norm is bounded uniformly for small $h$. Its $L^2_{\rm loc}$ limit is $u_s$. Apply the bounded-test Hilbert representation argument of [F2], after weight multiplication, simultaneously to the value and its first derivatives: local distributional convergence and the uniform global $H^1$ norm bound give bounded functionals on compact tests, hence global $L^2$ representatives with those bounds. Approximation of arbitrary $L^2$ tests by compact smooth tests then gives weak $H^1$ convergence. Thus $u_s$ lies in $H^1_\delta$ with the same bound and in the weakly closed weighted real boundary domain. The equation $u_t=-i(f-u_s)$ gives $u_t\in H^1_\delta$. Hence the remainder $r=u-\chi_+F$ belongs to $H^2_\delta$, with norm bounded by $C\|wf\|_{H^1}$. No normal derivative was constrained at the boundary. [F2, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

Iterate that tangential argument. Suppose the order-$q-1$ conclusion holds and $f\in H^q_\delta$, $q\ge2$. Step 5.1 already makes $u_s$ a weighted real-boundary section with zero constants, and its actual equation is $D_0u_s=f_s$. The integral of $(f_s)_0$ is zero: test its distributional derivative against longitudinal cutoffs tending to one, and use $f_0\in L^1$ and vanishing cutoff derivatives. Thus $u_s=Q_0f_s$ by uniqueness. Apply the order-$q-1$ conclusion to get $u_s\in H^q_\delta$ with its estimate. Then $u_t=-i(f-u_s)\in H^q_\delta$. Together with the known lower remainder norm and the compactly supported derivatives of $\chi_+F$, this proves $r\in H^{q+1}_\delta$ and $\|wr\|_{H^{q+1}}+|F|\le C_q\|wf\|_{H^q}$. Thus $Q_q$ is simply the restriction of the same $Q_0$ to $H^q_\delta$, with the claimed bound and no changed zeroth boundary domain. The case $q=0$ was step 4.1. The higher domain is closed and Hilbert because its weighted real $H^1$ condition is closed in the indicated higher norm, and its two constant coordinates are finite-dimensional. [F2, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct, algebra]

Boundedness of $D_0$ at every higher order follows by the same weighted derivative product rule and compact cutoff derivatives. Its range is all of $H^q_\delta$ by step 6.1 and its kernel remains the $m$-dimensional real constants, so it is Fredholm with index $m$. For a forcing of any indicated order, the exact matching condition from step 4.1 is necessary for both constants zero and sufficient because the specified $Q_q$ then has $F=0$; uniqueness follows from its global-constant kernel. Every construction was a prescribed Fourier sum, scalar primitive, contraction or bounded-test Hilbert representation under Countable Choice. This establishes the exact zero-mode neck inverse without inferring any nonlinear gluing or geometric bubble classification. [step 4.1, step 6.1, construct, algebra] ∎
